summary: This paper analyzes the energy consumption of the Semiclassical Quantum Fourier Transform on superconducting cat-qubit platforms, incorporating quantum error correction and comparing with classical FFT implementations. A quantum energetic advantage is found for systems with more than 26 logical qubits at the macroscopic level, arising before computational advantage and persisting with realistic cryogenic overhead.
motivation: Understanding whether quantum computing's algorithmic advantages translate to energy efficiency is essential as classical data centers face mounting power demands and quantum systems require substantial cryogenic and control infrastructure.
method: The authors computed microscopic, macroscopic (Carnot-efficiency cryogenics), and billed energy costs for cat-qubit gates ($Z(\theta)$, CNOT, measurement) with two-photon-driven dissipation stabilization ($\gamma_X \propto e^{-2\alpha^2}$, $\gamma_Z \propto \alpha^2$), developed an optimization procedure to minimize energy while maintaining final-qubit fidelity $F \geq 0.9$, and compared against state-of-the-art classical supercomputers (El Capitan: $1.641 \times 10^{-11}$ J/FLOP; KAIROS: $1.365 \times 10^{-11}$ J/FLOP).
result: Quantum energy consumption scales polynomially ($n^{3.06}$ macroscopic, $n^{2.81}$ microscopic optimized), while classical FFT scales exponentially, yielding energetic advantage at $n \geq 26$ qubits; this advantage emerges before temporal advantage ($n \gtrsim 34$–44 qubits), with stabilization energy dominating gate energy by orders of magnitude.
